identity.plain_name: A screw with two slightly different threads on it, so a full turn moves the part only by the tiny difference between them: a super-fine adjuster made from ordinary threads
aliases: differential micrometer / differential micrometer head (optics and measuring)
differential screw translator (Mitutoyo (brand) name for its extra-fine micrometer heads)
fine adjustment screw (the general name for fine adjusters; a differential screw is the extra-fine kind)
differential-pitch screw / headless compression screw, e.g. the Herbert screw (surgical bone screw)
identity.one_liner: One turn of a screw carrying two threads of slightly different pitch moves a nut that can't rotate by only the difference of the two pitches (for example M5 and M4 threads give 0.1 mm per turn), giving very fine, steady adjustment from coarse, standard threads.
identity.complexity: A few parts: a screw (spindle) with two threads of slightly different pitch, or two standard screws joined end to end, or a threaded sleeve with one pitch outside and another inside; a fixed nut; a second nut on the part being adjusted, kept from turning by a slot, square tube or guide; a knob or thimble; and often a small spring that pushes the moving nut to take up play.
identity.how_it_works: Turning the screw drives it through the fixed nut by one pitch, say 0.8 mm for an M5 thread. At the same time the second, finer thread on the same screw turns inside the moving nut, which can't rotate, and draws that nut back by its own pitch, 0.7 mm for M4. The moving nut therefore travels only the difference, 0.8 - 0.7 = 0.1 mm per turn, so a tenth of a turn moves it 10 um. Both threads must be the same hand (usually right-hand); with opposite hands the two movements add instead, as in a turnbuckle.

job: line parts up exactly: very fine position adjustment, e.g. optics, microscope focus, a 3D printer's Z endstop, measuring heads
change the kind of motion: rotation into a very small straight-line movement

change speed or turning force: in theory each turn gives a tiny movement and a large force (a 9:1 advantage over one of its threads alone in one example), though thread friction uses up much of that gain
finder_attributes.motion: rotate+slide: the knob and screw turn, and the output nut slides a small distance (e.g. 0.1 mm per turn); the total output range is usually only a few millimetres
finder_attributes.degrees_of_freedom: 1: the output nut's position is tied to the screw's rotation (one pitch difference per turn), so there is one independent motion
special_behaviour: motion conversion (rotary to linear): a turn of the knob becomes a very small straight movement of the output nut

self-locking (holds under load, won't back-drive): with a tiny effective lead and two pairs of sliding threads, pushing on the output can't turn the screw, so the setting stays put; a printed differential clamp maker calls this 'self-retention' (Printables, Jack)
holding_principle: shape (form-fit): both threads interlock with their nuts, so the output can only move when the screw is turned
friction or clamping (force-fit): friction in the two threads keeps the screw from turning back under load
finder_attributes.input_output: Rotation -> small straight-line motion. Effective pitch = P1 - P2 for single-start threads of the same hand: M5x0.8 with M4x0.7 gives 0.1 mm per turn; 16 tpi with 24 tpi gives about 0.0208 in (0.53 mm) per turn, the same as a 48 tpi thread; a 26 tpi thread with a 1.0 mm metric thread gives about 0.023 mm (Wikipedia). Force gain in theory = coarse pitch / difference, e.g. 9:1 over a 20 tpi screw for an 18/20 tpi pair (Home Metal Shop Club). Efficiency is low: the load presses on two sets of sliding threads, so the torque needed just to start turning is about double that of a single screw (Home Metal Shop Club). Shaft arrangement: in line. Back-drivable: no in practice (self-locking).
finder_attributes.power: passive (no power needed): usually turned by hand with a knob, thimble, wrench or socket; it can be motor-driven but rarely is
finder_attributes.removability: removable: the screw unscrews from both nuts; joined two-screw versions may be glued or thread-locked together
finder_attributes.reuse_cycles: many times: it is an adjuster made to be turned back and forth; nuts in plastic or brass slowly wear
finder_attributes.tools_needed: None to adjust (knob or thimble), or a wrench or socket for clamp versions. To make one: a tap and die (e.g. an M4 die), a lathe to turn down the end of a screw, or a coupling nut drilled and tapped to join two screws; thread-locker or epoxy to lock joined screws together (Rehorst; Hackaday).
finder_attributes.seal: none: nothing seals; the threads are open
finder_attributes.load: light: it is a fine adjuster for positioning, focusing and light clamping. Loads act along the screw (push or pull); keep bending and side loads off the fine threads by guiding the moving part. Clamping force by hand is limited because the friction of two threads doubles the starting torque (Home Metal Shop Club).
finder_attributes.adjustable: yes: adjustment is its whole purpose; the output is set by turning the knob, often after a coarse setting (differential micrometers combine a coarse micrometer drive with a fine differential drive)
finder_attributes.play_and_precision: Resolution is excellent: 0.1 mm per turn from M5/M4, so 10 um per tenth of a turn (Hackaday); Mitutoyo's differential micrometer heads have a 0.05 mm spindle pitch with 0.001 mm graduations (Mitutoyo). Backlash is noticeable unless handled: the play of the two threads adds together (Wikipedia 'Fine adjustment screw'), so push the moving nut against the thread with a spring (Rehorst) and approach the setting from one direction. Range is short: for 2 mm of output an M5/M4 screw must itself travel 16 mm (Rehorst). The moving nut must be guided so it can't rotate, and there is little tolerance for misalignment.
finder_attributes.access_needed: one side only (blind): it is adjusted by turning a knob or screw head from one side; assembly needs the nuts threaded on from the screw's ends
finder_attributes.materials: Screws: stainless steel (rigid; commonly 303) with brass nuts for low-cost greased adjusters or phosphor bronze for precise, hard-wearing ones (Wikipedia 'Fine adjustment screw'). DIY: standard steel machine screws with nuts embedded in printed parts, or with plastic (e.g. PTFE) blocks that the screw rolls its own thread into (Rehorst); coarse printed threads in PLA for demos and clamps (Printables).
finder_attributes.maker_difficulty: moderate: easy if you join two standard screws of different sizes with a drilled-and-tapped coupling nut or printed adapter, or print two coarse threads; moderate with a lathe (turn an M5 screw's end down and cut an M4 thread); sub-micron precision versions are bought

processes: off-the-shelf part (differential micrometer heads and differential adjuster screws for optical mounts)
3D print (FDM): coarse-thread differential clamps and demos, plus printed guides, nut holders and knobs for metal screws
CNC or manual lathe: turn down the end of a screw and cut a finer thread with a die, or drill and tap a coupling nut to join two screws
making.print_in_place: no: the screw, sleeve and nuts are printed or bought separately and screwed together; the moving nut also needs a separate anti-rotation guide
making.making_tips_3d_printing: 1) Let printed parts do the easy jobs and steel do the fine threads: Mark Rehorst's 3D printer Z-endstop uses a steel M5 screw turned down to M4 at one end, an M4 nut embedded in a printed 'flag', and a printed square tube that stops the flag rotating; a spring inside the tube pushes the flag against the nut to remove backlash. 2) Screws can roll their own threads in plastic: Rehorst drilled an undersized hole in a PTFE block for the M5 thread, giving a firm but adjustable fit; a commenter printed PETG parts and tapped most of the way through, leaving a few rolled threads to act like a lock washer. 3) No lathe? Hackaday suggests partly drilling and tapping a coupling nut, or printing an adapter that joins two bolts; lock the joint with thread-locker or epoxy (Rehorst). 4) Fully printed versions work with coarse threads: Sanford Prime's clamp uses 10 tpi and 13 tpi printed threads for roughly 44 tpi equivalent motion, printed in PLA; his first internal 1/2-13 thread needed a revised version, so print a test piece first. 5) Jack's printed clamp moves fast on a 10 mm pitch, then the second 8 mm-pitch thread takes over so the last half turn moves only 2 mm per turn with about 5x more force; he uses grease to keep friction low and leaves a 3.5 mm hole to glue in a reinforcing rod because printed layers are weak in tension. 6) Plan the thread lengths: with M5/M4 the screw moves 8 mm per 1 mm of output, so 2 mm of adjustment needs about 16 mm of M5 and 14 mm of M4 thread plus the nut thicknesses (Rehorst). 7) PLA softens above about 60 C (Prusa), so keep printed adjusters away from heated beds and motors.
making.off_the_shelf_parts: Differential micrometer heads (e.g. Mitutoyo Series 110 'differential screw translator' (brand), 0-1, 0-2.5 or 0-13 mm range); differential adjuster screws and differential drives for optical mounts and translation stages (optics suppliers); fine and ultra-fine adjustment screws with matched bushings (40-100 tpi and 100-508 tpi) when one fine thread is enough (Wikipedia); standard metric screws in pairs that differ by 0.1 mm of pitch (M3/M3.5, M3.5/M4, M4/M5) or 0.05 mm (M1.6/M2, M2/M2.5, M2.5/M3) (Rehorst); coupling nuts; taps and dies; small compression springs; thread-locker.
rules_of_thumb: Movement per turn = pitch 1 - pitch 2 for single-start threads of the same hand; in inches per turn it is 1/TPI1 - 1/TPI2 (Wikipedia 'Differential screw'). Examples: M5x0.8 with M4x0.7 = 0.1 mm per turn; 16 tpi with 24 tpi = about 0.0208 in per turn (like a 48 tpi thread) (Wikipedia).
Mixing metric and imperial threads gives still finer steps: 26 tpi (about 0.977 mm pitch) with a 1.0 mm metric thread = about 0.023 mm per turn (Wikipedia).
Standard metric pairs: M3/M3.5, M3.5/M4 and M4/M5 give 0.1 mm per turn; M1.6/M2, M2/M2.5 and M2.5/M3 give 0.05 mm per turn (Rehorst).

Output range is short: the screw itself moves (coarse pitch / difference) times the output, e.g. 8 mm of M5 travel per 1 mm of output with M5/M4, so 2 mm of adjustment needs about 16 mm of M5 and 14 mm of M4 thread (Rehorst).

Friction is the catch: the axial load bears on two threaded surfaces, so the torque to start turning is about twice that of a single screw, and the theoretical mechanical advantage (9:1 for an 18/20 tpi pair) does not help overcome it (Home Metal Shop Club, 2010).
Backlash from the two threads adds together (Wikipedia 'Fine adjustment screw'); preload the moving nut with a spring (Rehorst).
The moving nut must be stopped from rotating, or there is no differential action (Hackaday).

Threads finer than about 250 tpi (0.1 mm pitch) are hard to make, which is why differential adjusters are used for finer steps; lever or cone reducers are the other option (Wikipedia 'Fine adjustment screw').
Beware cheap 'differential screw micrometers' sold online that are only 0.5 mm pitch screws with a nice knob (Rehorst).

everyday_examples: Differential micrometer heads on laboratory and optical positioning stages, for sub-micrometre adjustment (Mitutoyo; Wikipedia)
A finely adjustable Z=0 endstop on a home-built 3D printer (Hackaday)
Headless 'compression' bone screws such as the Herbert screw, whose two ends have different thread pitches so tightening pulls the two bone pieces together (Wikipedia 'Herbert screw')
Historic machine levelling feet and astronomical micrometers (Wikipedia 'Differential screw')
guidance.when_to_use: Use it when you need very fine, steady adjustment that stays where you set it, but only have (or only want) coarse, strong, standard threads: focusing, aligning optics or lasers, setting an endstop or a bed height, fine feed of a tool, or a fine final tightening stage in a clamp. It is also the usual way to get steps finer than the finest threads that can be made, and a differential micrometer gives both a coarse and a fine knob in one unit.
guidance.when_not_to_use: Don't use it for long or fast travel: its range is short and each turn moves very little; use a lead screw or ball screw. Don't expect a big clamping force by hand, because friction on two threads doubles the starting torque (Home Metal Shop Club); use an ordinary screw clamp or a toggle clamp. If you need zero backlash, preload it with a spring or use a lever or flexure reducer instead (Wikipedia 'Fine adjustment screw'). If one fine thread is fine enough (e.g. an 80-100 tpi adjuster), that is simpler and cheaper.
guidance.environment_limits: Nothing special beyond ordinary threads: grit in fine threads makes them stick, and grease extends nut life, while phosphor bronze nuts can run without grease, e.g. in vacuum (Wikipedia 'Fine adjustment screw'). Superglue used to fix a ball tip on an adjuster can outgas and degrade over time (Wikipedia). Printed PLA parts soften above about 60 C (Prusa). At micrometre level, temperature changes of the screw and frame shift the setting [uncertain].
guidance.safety_notes: None known for small adjusters. A printed differential clamp can build up more force than its printed threads and layers can take (Jack reinforces his with a glued-in rod), so don't rely on printed clamps for anything hazardous.
guidance.common_failures: 1) The moving nut turns with the screw, so nothing happens or the part creeps; guide it with a slot or square tube (Hackaday; Rehorst). 2) Doubled backlash makes the setting jump when you reverse; add a spring and approach from one side (Rehorst; Wikipedia). 3) Too stiff to turn under load because of friction on two threads (Home Metal Shop Club); grease the threads (Printables, Jack). 4) Running out of range because the screw travels 8-10 times further than the output; plan thread lengths (Rehorst). 5) A joined two-part screw unscrews itself; use thread-locker or epoxy (Rehorst). 6) Printed internal threads come out wrong-sized; print a test first (Sanford Prime revised his). 7) Buying a fake 'differential micrometer' that is just a fine single thread (Rehorst).
related: Lead screw and nut: one thread, long travel; the basic screw drive this refines
Fine adjustment screw (single fine thread, 40-508 tpi): simpler, with less backlash, but threads finer than about 250 tpi are hard to get
Turnbuckle: two threads of opposite hand, so the movements add instead of subtract (fast take-up rather than fine adjustment)
Capstan and windlass, including the differential windlass: the same 'difference' trick with two rope drums of slightly different diameter
Parallel leaf-spring flexure (linear flexure stage): a bending stage, often with a lever that divides a screw's motion for backlash-free fine positioning
Eccentric adjuster: a turning off-centre bush for small, coarse-to-fine position tweaks
Kinematic coupling: fine adjusters usually push on kinematic mounts in optics
Compound planetary gearbox (split-ring / Wolfrom) and strain-wave gear: large reductions from the difference between two nearly equal tooth counts
